07-glacial-landscapes.explain: Internal deformation is what happens where it is too cold for basal flow. Gravity causes the compressed ice to flow over the lip of the hollow it formed in.

07-glacial-landscapes.q: What proportion of houses in the Lake District are second homes?
07-glacial-landscapes.explain: 20%, which is the clearest figure for the social impact of tourism: second homeowners can price out locals, and villages lose the permanent residents the local services depend on.

07-glacial-landscapes.q: Why do most UK corries face north or east?
options: the prevailing wind blows the ice in that direction
these slopes are steeper, so ice can accumulate more easily
north- and east-facing slopes are shaded, so snow survives the summer and can compress into ice
the rock on these slopes is softer and erodes faster
07-glacial-landscapes.explain: On a south-facing slope the snow melts each year, so it never accumulates and no glacier forms. East-facing slopes also collect snow blown over the ridge by the prevailing south-westerly wind.

07-glacial-landscapes.q: AQA defines till as…
options: material, chiefly sand or gravel, deposited by meltwater streams
frost-shattered debris carried on the surface of a glacier
a large boulder carried far from its source region
an unsorted mixture of sand, clay and boulders carried by a glacier and deposited as ground moraine over a large area
07-glacial-landscapes.explain: Unsorted is the examined word: ice carries everything at once and, being solid, cannot sort by size or round the fragments. Option 1 is outwash and option 3 an erratic.

07-glacial-landscapes.q: Outwash differs from till because outwash is…
options: sorted and rounded, because it is deposited by meltwater streams
angular and unsorted, because it is deposited directly by ice
found only beneath the glacier, never in front of it
made up entirely of boulders too large for meltwater to move
07-glacial-landscapes.explain: Water's carrying capacity depends on particle size and velocity, so it drops the heaviest material first and carries the finest furthest, and attrition in transport rounds the fragments. That is why the 2019 data showed a sediment range of 25.3 cm on the till plain against 6.6 cm on the outwash plain.

07-glacial-landscapes.q: Why is the material deposited by a glacier mixed in size and shape?
options: the glacier picks up material from several different rock types
ice carries material on its surface, inside itself and at its base all at once and, being solid, cannot sort it by size
meltwater mixes the material as the glacier retreats
bulldozing crushes large boulders into smaller fragments
07-glacial-landscapes.explain: This was 2022 Q05.5. Ice has no sorting mechanism and does not round the fragments by attrition, because they are locked in place rather than knocking against one another — which is exactly what makes till unsorted and angular.

07-glacial-landscapes.q: AQA defines a corrie as…
options: a long, narrow lake found on the floor of a glaciated valley
a sharp, knife-like ridge formed between two corries
an armchair-shaped hollow in the mountainside formed by glacial erosion, rotational slip and freeze-thaw weathering
a river valley widened and deepened into a U-shape by a glacier
07-glacial-landscapes.explain: The definition adds that this is where the valley glacier begins, and that when the ice melts it can leave a small circular lake called a tarn. Option 2 is an arête and option 4 a glacial trough.

07-glacial-landscapes.q: What is tourism worth to the Lake District each year?
options: £5bn
£2.3bn and 75 000 jobs
07-glacial-landscapes.explain: That is the economic benefit to weigh against footpath erosion, boat pollution in Windermere, congestion in Ambleside and 20% second homes. Coniferous forestry is the £30m figure; £5bn is the value of tourism protected at Brighton.

07-glacial-landscapes.q: Why does a corrie have a lip at its downhill end?
options: the ice is thinner there so moves more slowly and erodes less, and frost-shattered rock may be deposited there
the rock at the front of the hollow is always more resistant
meltwater deposits a ridge of outwash across the exit
rotational slip lifts material up and over the front edge
07-glacial-landscapes.explain: The lip is what dams the meltwater to form a tarn once the ice has gone. The lip and the tarn are the two easiest extra marks on a corrie question and are routinely left out.

07-glacial-landscapes.q: An arête is…
options: a steep pyramid-shaped summit where several corries meet
a sharp, knife-like ridge formed between two corries cutting back by erosion and freeze-thaw
a former river spur sliced off by a valley glacier
a tributary valley left high above the main valley floor
07-glacial-landscapes.explain: Striding Edge on Helvellyn is the school's Lake District example. Option 1 is a pyramidal peak, option 3 a truncated spur and option 4 a hanging valley.

07-glacial-landscapes.q: A pyramidal peak forms where…
options: two corries cut back towards each other on opposite sides of a ridge
a glacier over-deepens the floor of its trough
several corries cut back to meet at a central point, leaving a steep pyramid
freeze-thaw weathering shatters a summit into angular blocks
07-glacial-landscapes.explain: Two corries back to back give an arête; three or more meeting at a point give a pyramidal peak. Both are produced by the same back-wall retreat that forms the corries themselves.

07-glacial-landscapes.q: Why does a glacier produce a U-shaped valley where a river produces a V-shaped one?
options: glacial ice is denser than water, so it erodes downwards more strongly
glaciers only occupy valleys that were already wide
rivers erode in summer only, whereas glaciers erode all year
the ice fills the whole valley and is rigid, so it erodes the sides as well as the floor and cannot flow around obstacles
07-glacial-landscapes.explain: That one sentence explains the U-shape, the truncated spurs and the straightening of the valley at once. A river occupies only a narrow channel, so it erodes downwards and flows round obstacles, leaving interlocking spurs.

07-glacial-landscapes.q: A truncated spur is…
options: a former river valley spur which has been sliced off by a valley glacier, forming cliff-like edges
a ridge of till deposited along the side of a glacier
an isolated hill of rock left standing in the middle of a glacial trough
the steep back wall of a corrie after the ice has melted
07-glacial-landscapes.explain: Because the rigid ice filled the valley it could not flow around the interlocking spurs of the old river valley, so it cut straight through them.

07-glacial-landscapes.q: A hanging valley is…
options: a valley dammed by a terminal moraine so that it holds a lake
a tributary valley eroded much less than the main valley, left high above its floor and often the site of a waterfall
a valley whose floor has been over-deepened into a ribbon lake
the upper part of a glacial trough above the former snow line
07-glacial-landscapes.explain: AQA's definition adds that it was too cold and high up for ice to move easily, so it was not eroded as much as the lower main valley — hence the waterfall crashing several hundred metres to the main valley floor.

07-glacial-landscapes.q: A ribbon lake is a long, narrow lake formed where…
options: a terminal moraine dams the mouth of a glacial trough
meltwater ponds behind an outwash plain
the glacier had more erosive power, so the valley floor was over-deepened
two glaciers merged and their medial moraine blocked the valley
07-glacial-landscapes.explain: AQA gives three reasons the glacier might have had more erosive power there: softer rock, a temporarily steeper valley gradient, or a tributary glacier joining and adding ice. Ullswater is the school's Lake District example and Llyn Ogwen was the 2023 paper's.

07-glacial-landscapes.q: A medial moraine forms where…
options: the glacier snout bulldozes material across the valley at its furthest advance
freeze-thaw debris falls onto the edge of a glacier from the valley sides
basal material is released as a sheet across the valley floor
a tributary glacier joins the main glacier and their two adjoining lateral moraines merge into one central ridge
07-glacial-landscapes.explain: Option 1 is a terminal moraine, option 2 a lateral moraine and option 3 ground moraine. All four are unsorted till, because ice does not sort or round its load.

07-glacial-landscapes.q: A terminal moraine marks…
options: the furthest point the glacier snout reached, as a ridge of unsorted till across the valley
the boundary between the till plain and the outwash plain at the valley sides
the line along which two glaciers merged
the upper limit of ice in the valley
07-glacial-landscapes.explain: The snout bulldozes material forward by the sheer weight of the ice, and melting at the point of maximum advance releases it as a ridge. Beyond it, meltwater streams build the sorted, rounded outwash plain.

07-glacial-landscapes.q: Which description of a drumlin's shape is correct?
options: a rounded hill or bump of till with no clear orientation
elongated or oval, with a steep blunt end facing up-ice and a long tapering tail down-ice
a sharp conical mound of sorted sand and gravel
a long low ridge running across the direction of ice flow
07-glacial-landscapes.explain: The school's feedback lesson states that a 'hill' or 'bump' does not refer to the correct shape. The long axis is parallel to the former direction of ice, which is why drumlins occur in aligned swarms — basket-of-eggs topography.

07-glacial-landscapes.q: What is the name given to a large boulder transported and deposited by glaciers in areas with a different rock type?
options: Moraine
Outwash
Erratic
Till
07-glacial-landscapes.explain: This was 2023 Q05.1. The giveaway in the stem is 'a different rock type' — because its rock does not match the local bedrock, an erratic records the direction the ice came from.

07-glacial-landscapes.q: Striding Edge in the Lake District is an example of which landform?
options: a corrie
a ribbon lake
a drumlin
an arête
07-glacial-landscapes.explain: The school's Lake District set is: arête Striding Edge, ribbon lake Ullswater, corrie Blea Water, U-shaped valley Langdale (all erosion), and drumlins at Swindale (deposition).

07-glacial-landscapes.q: How many tourists visit the Lake District each year?
options: 18 million
1.8 million
07-glacial-landscapes.explain: 18 million, against just 40 000 local people — roughly 450 visitors per resident, which is the ratio that explains footpath erosion, congestion and the second-home problem. The school's model answer quotes 18.4 million.

07-glacial-landscapes.q: The Honister Slate Mine in the Lake District is significant because it…
options: was closed by the National Park authority to protect the landscape
combines working quarrying with tourism, offering climbing and a 1 km zip-wire
is the site of the Fix the Fells footpath repair scheme
imposes a 10 knot speed limit to protect the lake
07-glacial-landscapes.explain: It shows development and conservation are not always opposed — which is the direct comparison for the 2023 question on the contested zip wire proposed across the Thirlmere Valley. The 10 knot limit applies to boats on Lake Windermere.

08-urban-issues-and-challenges.q: Urbanisation is best defined as…
options: the increase in the proportion of a population living in towns and cities
the absolute increase in the size of a city
the movement of people from one country to another
the spread of a city into the surrounding countryside
08-urban-issues-and-challenges.explain: Urbanisation is a proportion. An absolute increase in city size is urban growth, and spread into the countryside is urban sprawl — AQA asked for this exact definition for 1 mark in 2025.

08-urban-issues-and-challenges.q: A megacity is an urban area with a population of at least…
options: 1 million
5 million
10 million
20 million
08-urban-issues-and-challenges.explain: AQA's own wording is "in excess of ten million people". There were 33 megacities in 2023 and around 50 are expected by 2050.

08-urban-issues-and-challenges.q: What proportion of the world's increased urban population is expected to be in Africa and Asia?
08-urban-issues-and-challenges.explain: 90% — one of the school's own recall facts. It is why the LIC/NEE city case study carries so much of Section A.

08-urban-issues-and-challenges.q: Which region is the most urbanised in the world?
options: Western Europe
North America, at about 82%
East Asia
Australasia
08-urban-issues-and-challenges.explain: North America is the most urbanised region, with roughly 82% of its population in urban areas; HICs generally are at least 75% urban.

08-urban-issues-and-challenges.q: Which three countries are expected to account for 37% of the growth in the world's urban population between 2014 and 2050?
options: India, China and Nigeria
Brazil, Indonesia and Egypt
China, the USA and Pakistan
Nigeria, Bangladesh and Mexico
08-urban-issues-and-challenges.explain: India, China and Nigeria. The combination of huge populations and rapid rural–urban migration concentrates global urban growth in these three.

08-urban-issues-and-challenges.q: The two factors that affect the rate of urbanisation are…
options: birth rate and counter-urbanisation
natural increase and urban sprawl
industrialisation and gentrification
migration and natural increase
08-urban-issues-and-challenges.explain: Migration and natural increase. They are linked: migrants are typically aged 18–35, so the birth rate rises and the death rate stays low.

08-urban-issues-and-challenges.q: Rio de Janeiro has grown up around which feature?
options: Guanabara Bay, a large natural bay
Lake Titicaca
The mouth of the Amazon
The Paraná delta
08-urban-issues-and-challenges.explain: Guanabara Bay in south-east Brazil. The bay is also where the city's water pollution problem concentrates — 150 tonnes a day.

08-urban-issues-and-challenges.q: Roughly how many people live in the Greater Rio de Janeiro metropolitan area?
options: 6 million
9 million
13 million
22 million
08-urban-issues-and-challenges.explain: 13 million in Greater Rio, of whom around 1.5 million live in favelas — about 24% of the city, across roughly 1,000 favelas.

08-urban-issues-and-challenges.q: Rio de Janeiro's national importance includes which figure?
options: 22% of Brazil's GNI and the largest port in Brazil
5% of Brazil's GNI and the 3rd busiest port in Brazil
Brazil's capital city since 1960
40% of Brazil's manufacturing output
08-urban-issues-and-challenges.explain: 5% of Brazil's GNI and the third busiest port. It is also Brazil's second most important industrial centre — and Brasília, not Rio, is the capital.

08-urban-issues-and-challenges.q: Infant mortality in the Cidade de Deus favela compared with the wealthy district of Barra is…
options: 9 per 1,000 against 21 per 1,000
94 per 1,000 against 5 per 1,000
roughly the same in both
21 per 1,000 against 9 per 1,000
08-urban-issues-and-challenges.explain: 21 per 1,000 in Cidade de Deus against 9 in Barra. Favela residents also live about 13 years less than people in wealthier parts of Rio.

08-urban-issues-and-challenges.q: What percentage of children in Rio continue in education beyond the age of 14?
options: About 50%
About 70%
About 90%
About 97%
08-urban-issues-and-challenges.explain: Only about 50%, despite Rio having over 400 secondary schools, 6 universities and a 97% literacy rate — the classic "opportunity exists but is unevenly shared" contrast.

08-urban-issues-and-challenges.q: The Guandu water treatment plant in Rio is notable because it is…
options: the largest water treatment plant in the world
Brazil's oldest treatment works
entirely solar powered
funded by the Favela-Bairro Project
08-urban-issues-and-challenges.explain: The world's largest, supplying the great majority of Rio's fresh water — yet 12% of favela homes still lack running water and a third of supply is lost to leaks, fraud and illegal access.

08-urban-issues-and-challenges.q: Which scheme supplies around 30% of Rio's energy?
options: The Ternium Steelworks generator
The Seropédica landfill gas plant
The Santa Marta solar panels
The Simplício hydro-electric plant
08-urban-issues-and-challenges.explain: The Simplício HEP plant, built at a cost of $2 billion and opened in 2013, supplies about 30% of Rio's energy.

08-urban-issues-and-challenges.q: Roughly how many people work in Rio's informal economy, and for about how much?
options: 3.5 million for about £75 a month
350,000 for about £75 a month
3.5 million for about £750 a month
1.5 million for about £300 a month
08-urban-issues-and-challenges.explain: 3.5 million people on about £75 a month. Informal workers pay no tax, which starves the city of revenue — the key disadvantage of the informal economy.

08-urban-issues-and-challenges.q: Air pollution caused largely by congestion in Rio causes approximately how many deaths a year?
08-urban-issues-and-challenges.explain: About 5,000 a year. Rio is the most congested city in South America and car ownership rose 40% in ten years — an environmental challenge affecting the whole city, not just the favelas.

08-urban-issues-and-challenges.q: What proportion of Rio's waste is recycled?
options: About 50%
Less than 2%
About 35%
About 20%
08-urban-issues-and-challenges.explain: Less than 2%. Most goes to the Seropédica landfill 70 km away, where landfill gas is captured to generate electricity or fuel the collection vehicles.

08-urban-issues-and-challenges.q: The Favela-Bairro Project ran from…
08-urban-issues-and-challenges.explain: 1995–2009, a site and service scheme costing the government $1 billion and helping 250,000 people across more than 100 favelas.

08-urban-issues-and-challenges.q: Which measure is usually identified as the most important thing the Favela-Bairro Project did?
options: Giving residents legal ownership of the land they lived on
Building the Complexo do Alemão cable car
Installing 60 km of power cables
Establishing Pacifying Police Units
08-urban-issues-and-challenges.explain: Legal land title, plus 100% mortgages and low-interest loans, gave residents a reason to invest in homes they could no longer be evicted from — so they rebuilt in brick.

08-urban-issues-and-challenges.q: Before the Favela-Bairro Project, what proportion of non-improved favelas had no sewage connection?
08-urban-issues-and-challenges.explain: 50% had no sewage connection and 30% had no electricity. The project built 12 new sewage works and installed 60 km of new power cables.

08-urban-issues-and-challenges.q: A criticism of the Favela-Bairro Project is that…
options: it demolished favelas rather than upgrading them
funding was reduced after 2008, so long-term sustainability is doubtful
it refused to give residents legal land title
it was funded entirely by foreign TNCs
08-urban-issues-and-challenges.explain: Funding fell after 2008; improvements were also uneven with some favelas left out, pacification displaced residents, and some new pavements raised flood risk on steep slopes.

08-urban-issues-and-challenges.q: What percentage of London's population was born outside the UK?
08-urban-issues-and-challenges.explain: 37%. London's migrant streams were dominated by the former British Empire after WWII and by Eastern Europe after EU free movement in 2007.

08-urban-issues-and-challenges.q: London generates approximately what share of the UK's GNI?
08-urban-issues-and-challenges.explain: 22% of UK GNI. Average earnings are also about £6,000 a year higher in London, and the city attracts 30 million tourists a year through 6 major airports.

08-urban-issues-and-challenges.q: The life expectancy gap between Chelsea and Tower Hamlets is…
options: 84 years against 82 years
80 years against 74 years
88 years against 56 years
88 years against 80 years
08-urban-issues-and-challenges.explain: 88 in Chelsea against 80 in Tower Hamlets, which also has the highest poverty rate of any London borough at 56%.

08-urban-issues-and-challenges.q: London's homeless population of around 170,000 represents roughly what share of the UK total?
08-urban-issues-and-challenges.explain: About half the UK total. Average house prices are over £500,000 and rough sleeping has risen 23% since 2020.

08-urban-issues-and-challenges.q: A brownfield site is best defined as…
options: land that has been used, abandoned and now awaits some new use
land on the rural–urban fringe that has never been built on
any derelict building in a city centre
farmland bought by a developer
08-urban-issues-and-challenges.explain: AQA's wording exactly, and it is commonly found in the inner city. London had almost 3,000 brownfield sites covering 2,600 hectares in 2019.

08-urban-issues-and-challenges.q: Before regeneration, Stratford in east London was notable as…
options: London's largest area of greenfield land
the most polluted site in Western Europe
the borough with the highest house prices
the site of London's main container port
08-urban-issues-and-challenges.explain: The most polluted site in Western Europe, with derelict industries, poor transport links and one of the most deprived communities in the country.

08-urban-issues-and-challenges.q: How much green space does the Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park contain?
options: 10 hectares
27 hectares
100 hectares
250 hectares
08-urban-issues-and-challenges.explain: 100 hectares of green space within the 250-hectare park. The International Quarter holds 25,000 workers and over 20,000 jobs are expected by 2030, bringing more than £5 billion.

08-urban-issues-and-challenges.q: East Village in Stratford reduces water consumption by roughly how much compared with the average?
08-urban-issues-and-challenges.explain: 50% less water, through rainwater harvesting and grey water recycling, and 30% less energy from a biomass Combined Heat and Power system. 99% is the parkland waste recycling figure.

08-urban-issues-and-challenges.q: CHP, used at East Village, stands for…
options: Controlled Hydro Production
Carbon Housing Programme
Community Heating Project
Combined Heat and Power
08-urban-issues-and-challenges.explain: Combined Heat and Power generates electricity and useful heat simultaneously, so far less energy is wasted than in a conventional power station.

08-urban-issues-and-challenges.q: By how much did NO₂ levels fall in London's original ULEZ zone?
08-urban-issues-and-challenges.explain: 44%. The Congestion Charge figure is a 30% fall in central traffic since 2003, and 66% is the share of London's waste sent to incineration in 2021.

09-the-changing-economic-world.q: Which measure of development combines income, life expectancy and education levels?
options: The Human Development Index
Infant mortality rate
GNI
The Demographic Transition Model
09-the-changing-economic-world.explain: HDI combines GDP per capita, life expectancy and adult literacy into a single index. AQA asked this for 1 mark in 2023.

09-the-changing-economic-world.q: Gross national income (GNI) differs from GDP because it also includes…
options: government spending
income earned from investments overseas
the value of unpaid work
the informal economy
09-the-changing-economic-world.explain: GNI takes into account not just goods and services but income earned from investments overseas, then divides by population.

09-the-changing-economic-world.q: The main limitation of every economic and social measure of development is that…
options: they cannot be compared between countries
the data is always out of date
they only apply to HICs
they are averages for the whole country, so they hide internal inequality
09-the-changing-economic-world.explain: Averages describe nobody: Nigeria's GDP per head is US$3,617 in the south and US$292 in its poorest region. This is the reason examiners want for any "limitations" question.

09-the-changing-economic-world.q: Why can an HIC have a higher death rate than an LIC?
options: Death rate depends on age structure, and HICs have far more elderly people
Healthcare is worse in HICs
LICs do not record deaths
HICs have higher infant mortality
09-the-changing-economic-world.explain: A crude death rate reflects age structure: Japan has 28% over 65, so its death rate is high even though life expectancy is among the world's highest. Infant mortality is the better health indicator.

09-the-changing-economic-world.q: Infant mortality in Nigeria and the UK is approximately…
options: 47 and 93 per 1,000 live births
94 and 5 per 1,000 live births
54 and 81 per 1,000 live births
21 and 9 per 1,000 live births
09-the-changing-economic-world.explain: 94 against 5. Life expectancy is 54 against 81, internet users 47% against 93%, and HDI rank 164th against 13th.

09-the-changing-economic-world.q: Which stage of the Demographic Transition Model is Japan in?
options: Stage 2, early expanding
Stage 3, late expanding
Stage 4, low fluctuating
Stage 5, natural decrease
09-the-changing-economic-world.explain: Stage 5: the death rate slightly exceeds the birth rate, so the population falls and ages. In 2020 Japan had 12% under 15 and 28% over 65.

09-the-changing-economic-world.q: In Stage 2 of the DTM, population rises rapidly because…
options: the death rate falls while the birth rate stays high
the birth rate rises sharply
both rates fall together
migration increases
09-the-changing-economic-world.explain: Clean water, better food supply and basic medicine cut deaths, but attitudes to family size have not yet changed — so births greatly exceed deaths.

09-the-changing-economic-world.q: The economic benefit of Stage 3 is that…
options: the total population finally stops growing
the working-age population grows relative to dependents
life expectancy exceeds 80
the death rate falls below the birth rate
09-the-changing-economic-world.explain: The demographic dividend: the large Stage 2 cohort reaches working age as the birth rate falls, so there are more workers and fewer dependents, more women in paid work, and more income available to save, invest or tax.

09-the-changing-economic-world.q: Which of these is a PHYSICAL cause of uneven development?
options: Being landlocked, so there is no port for trade
Colonialism
Government corruption
Reliance on low-value primary exports
09-the-changing-economic-world.explain: Physical causes are weather and climate, relief, being landlocked, tropical disease environments and water shortages. Trade is economic and colonialism historical.

09-the-changing-economic-world.q: How many people died of malaria in 2019?
options: 4 million
09-the-changing-economic-world.explain: 400,000, almost all in LICs — the standard figure for disparities in health as a consequence of uneven development.

09-the-changing-economic-world.q: What share of global wealth is held in North America?
09-the-changing-economic-world.explain: 34% of global wealth in a region with a small fraction of the world's people — the headline figure for disparities in wealth.

09-the-changing-economic-world.q: Debt relief reduces the development gap by…
options: cancelling money already owed, so repayments can fund development instead
lending money at a lower rate of interest
giving goods and services rather than cash
guaranteeing a fair price for exports
09-the-changing-economic-world.explain: Cancellation, not lending — the 2023 examiner's report says candidates routinely conflated debt relief with loans. $75 billion was written off across the 19 HIPCs.

09-the-changing-economic-world.q: Total debt relief across the 19 Heavily Indebted Poor Countries amounted to…
options: $7.5 billion
$12.5 billion
$34 billion
$75 billion
09-the-changing-economic-world.explain: $75 billion. $12.5 billion is the Grameen Bank's total lending and $34 billion is Peru's projected earnings from Camisea.

09-the-changing-economic-world.q: Intermediate technology is best described as…
options: simple, easily learned and maintained technology serving local needs
the most advanced technology available
second-hand machinery donated by HICs
technology halfway between manual and automated
09-the-changing-economic-world.explain: AQA's definition. The point is that it can be repaired locally without imported parts or outside expertise — which is why Chambamontera's micro-hydro scheme is sustainable.

09-the-changing-economic-world.q: What proportion of small coffee farmers in eastern Uganda have joined the Gumutindo Co-operative?
09-the-changing-economic-world.explain: 90%. Collective organisation gives Fairtrade farmers the scale to negotiate and export directly, on top of the guaranteed price and the community premium.

09-the-changing-economic-world.q: Tourism contributed approximately what share of Jamaica's GDP in 2019?
09-the-changing-economic-world.explain: 35% of GDP, from 4 million visitors a year, generating about $2 billion and over 50% of Jamaica's total foreign exchange earnings.

09-the-changing-economic-world.q: Roughly how many Jamaicans are employed directly and indirectly in tourism?
options: 2 million
09-the-changing-economic-world.explain: Over 200,000 — tourism is the country's main source of employment and its second largest employer.

09-the-changing-economic-world.q: Which of these is a genuine limitation of tourism-led development in Jamaica?
options: Visitor numbers have fallen every year since 1994
Tourism employs fewer than 10,000 people
The government banned cruise ships at Falmouth
Wealthy areas such as Montego Bay have benefited most, and pockets of poverty persist
09-the-changing-economic-world.explain: The benefits are geographically concentrated, and roads for residents came late because ports and airports were prioritised. Growth in arrivals also slowed in 2009 because of the recession abroad.

09-the-changing-economic-world.q: Nigeria borders which group of countries?
options: Benin, Niger, Chad and Cameroon
Ghana, Togo and Mali
Sudan, Chad and Libya
Senegal, Guinea and Liberia
09-the-changing-economic-world.explain: Benin, Niger, Chad and Cameroon, with the Gulf of Guinea to the south. It is in West Africa.

09-the-changing-economic-world.q: Nigeria became independent of the UK in…
09-the-changing-economic-world.explain: 1960. Its political and trading links ran almost entirely to the UK before that; it now trades most with the EU, USA and India, with links to China growing.

09-the-changing-economic-world.q: Oil accounts for what share of Nigeria's GDP and export earnings respectively?
options: 98% of GDP and 14% of exports
14% of GDP and 98% of exports
27% of GDP and 53% of exports
2.2% of GDP and 40% of exports
09-the-changing-economic-world.explain: 14% of GDP but 98% of export earnings — which is why the whole economy is exposed to the world oil price despite oil being a small part of domestic activity.

09-the-changing-economic-world.q: Nigeria's service sector now accounts for roughly what share of its economy?
09-the-changing-economic-world.explain: 53%, with manufacturing at 27% and growing fastest. Employment in agriculture has fallen by 40% through mechanisation and better pay elsewhere.

09-the-changing-economic-world.q: Shell began operating in Nigeria in…
09-the-changing-economic-world.explain: 1958, with the discovery of oil and controversial extraction operations in the Niger Delta.

09-the-changing-economic-world.q: Which of these is an ADVANTAGE of Shell to Nigeria?
options: It is registered in Bermuda
Gas flaring reduced air pollution
Oil spills at Bodo cleaned the Niger Delta
Around 90% of its contracts are awarded to Nigerian companies
09-the-changing-economic-world.explain: Around 90% of contracts to local firms (AQA's 2025 scheme gives 91%), plus $250,000 on healthcare and 3,000 school scholarships. Bermuda registration is a disadvantage, because less tax is paid.

09-the-changing-economic-world.q: How many residents took out a lawsuit against Shell over oil pollution in Ogoniland?
09-the-changing-economic-world.explain: 42,000. Contamination in Ogoniland is 1,000 times higher than elsewhere, following two massive spills at Bodo in the Niger Delta.

09-the-changing-economic-world.q: What percentage of Nigeria's forests have been destroyed by logging, agriculture and urban expansion?
09-the-changing-economic-world.explain: 96%. 94% is the share of the population exposed to high air pollution, and 60% is the share living in poverty.

09-the-changing-economic-world.q: Between 1990 and 2019, Nigeria's access to safe water rose from…
09-the-changing-economic-world.explain: 46% to 85% — paired with a 9-year rise in life expectancy between 2015 and 2019, these are the quality-of-life gains that stop a Nigeria answer being one-sided.

09-the-changing-economic-world.q: De-industrialisation is defined as the decline of traditional manufacturing due to…
options: government policy alone
exhaustion of raw materials, loss of markets and competition from NEEs
a falling birth rate
the growth of science parks
09-the-changing-economic-world.explain: AQA's own definition. In the UK it meant the decline of coal mining, shipbuilding and steel, with a negative multiplier effect as suppliers closed too — North East England was worst hit.

09-the-changing-economic-world.q: Approximately what share of the UK economy comes from the tertiary sector?
09-the-changing-economic-world.explain: 80% tertiary, with 1.7% from research. 1.3 million people work in IT, and digital technology turnover grew 2.6 times faster than UK GDP in 2016–17.

09-the-changing-economic-world.q: Torr Quarry in Somerset contributes how much a year to the local economy, and how much land has been landscaped?
options: £15 million a year, 2.5 hectares landscaped
£150 million a year, 8 hectares landscaped
£1.5 million a year, 800 hectares landscaped
£15 million a year, 80 hectares landscaped
09-the-changing-economic-world.explain: £15 million a year and 80 hectares landscaped, with the Somerset Wildlife Trust creating biodiverse-rich landscapes. 2.5 km² is the size of the quarry itself.

10-resource-management.q: In Section C of Paper 2, which questions should you answer?
options: Question 03 and one of Questions 04, 05 or 06
Question 03 only
All of Questions 03 to 06
Questions 04, 05 and 06 only
10-resource-management.explain: Question 03 is compulsory, then one option: 04 Food, 05 Water or 06 Energy. Your class does Energy — and Q03 covers UK food, water AND energy regardless.

10-resource-management.q: Resource management is defined as…
options: the extraction of resources for profit
the control and monitoring of resources so they do not become depleted or exhausted
the transfer of resources between countries
reducing the use of non-renewable resources to zero
10-resource-management.explain: AQA's wording. A resource itself is "something which human society attaches value to due to its usefulness".

10-resource-management.q: Which regions are described as prone to water shortages and drought?
options: Europe, South East Asia and northern North America
South America and Central Asia
North America and East Asia
Africa, the Middle East and Australia
10-resource-management.explain: Africa, the Middle East and Australia. Europe, South East Asia, northern South America and northern North America have a water surplus.

10-resource-management.q: Roughly how many countries face food insecurity?
10-resource-management.explain: About 50 countries, and more than 800 million people live every day with hunger or food insecurity. The food deficit regions are sub-Saharan Africa plus India, Pakistan, Bangladesh and Afghanistan.

10-resource-management.q: What percentage of the food eaten in the UK comes from LICs?
10-resource-management.explain: 12% — which raises food miles and the carbon footprint of the UK diet. Coincidentally, 12% of UK greenhouse gas emissions also come from agriculture itself.

10-resource-management.q: Food miles means…
options: the distance covered supplying food to consumers
the distance a farmer travels to market
the carbon emitted per kilogram of food
the area of land needed to feed one person
10-resource-management.explain: AQA's definition. Local food sourcing cuts food miles — but out-of-season UK produce grown in heated glasshouses can still have a high footprint.

10-resource-management.q: Organic produce is defined partly by the fact that…
options: it is always grown within 50 miles of the consumer
artificial fertilisers are banned and fertility is built by crop rotation, compost, manure and clover
it uses hydroponics rather than soil
it is grown only in greenhouses
10-resource-management.explain: No artificial fertilisers and no synthetic additives such as pesticides and dyes; soil fertility comes from rotation, compost, manure and clover.

10-resource-management.q: Agribusiness increases food production mainly because…
options: it uses only organic methods
it relies on hand labour rather than machines
it reduces the amount of land farmed
farming takes place on a greater scale, with hedgerows removed and more mechanisation and chemicals
10-resource-management.explain: Larger farms created by combining fields and removing hedgerows, with greater use of mechanisation and chemicals to raise yields — at the cost of habitat and chemical runoff.

10-resource-management.q: Why does the UK need water transfer schemes even though it receives enough rainfall overall?
options: Rainfall is greatest in the west while demand is greatest in the drier south-east
Rainfall has declined every year since 1990
All UK rainfall falls in winter
The UK exports most of its water
10-resource-management.explain: A spatial mismatch: the wettest region is the west, the highest demand is in the south-east, which is also the driest and runs a water deficit — so water is transferred between river basins.

10-resource-management.q: Average daily water consumption per person in the UK is about…
options: 31 litres
150 litres
310 litres
970 litres
10-resource-management.explain: 310 litres a day, and demand is expected to exceed supply by 2034. Dishwasher ownership rose from 22% in 1998 to 49% in 2018.

10-resource-management.q: Eutrophication in UK rivers is caused by…
options: oil and heavy metals from transport
nutrients from fertiliser and sewage producing algae that reduce oxygen levels
plastic microbeads blocking the river bed
warm water discharged from power stations
10-resource-management.explain: Nutrients from farmland and sewage feed algal growth, which depletes dissolved oxygen and kills fish — causing economic losses to fishermen and tourism.

10-resource-management.q: What proportion of UK energy was 'green' in 2020?
10-resource-management.explain: 47% in 2020. 35% was the share imported in 2019, and 65% is the renewables target for 2030.

10-resource-management.q: Which statement best describes the UK's changing energy mix?
options: A shift from fossil fuels and nuclear towards renewables, with nuclear falling only slightly
A shift from renewables back to gas
A shift from nuclear to coal
No significant change in the last 30 years
10-resource-management.explain: Fossil fuel use has fallen because of environmental impact and declining domestic supplies; renewables have risen for environmental benefit and carbon targets; nuclear has fallen slightly.

10-resource-management.q: Approximately how much does a new nuclear power station cost to build?
options: £4 million
£22 million
£2.2 billion
£22 billion
10-resource-management.explain: About £22 billion, against roughly £4 million for a commercial wind turbine — high set-up costs are the main economic barrier to new low-carbon capacity.

10-resource-management.q: Energy security is defined as…
options: the uninterrupted availability of energy sources at an affordable price
generating all of a country's energy domestically
having enough fossil fuel reserves to last 50 years
having no power cuts in a given year
10-resource-management.explain: Both halves matter — uninterrupted AND affordable — which is why an HIC with plenty of supply can still be insecure when prices spike.

10-resource-management.q: Energy insecurity is best defined as…
options: an energy deficit, where demand exceeds supply
when energy availability is not enough to ensure good health, livelihood and earnings
the absence of any renewable generation
importing more than half of a country's energy
10-resource-management.explain: AQA's wording. The 2023 examiner's report notes the only common error was candidates defining an energy DEFICIT instead.

10-resource-management.q: Which of these are the three drivers of rising global energy consumption?
options: Industrialisation, deforestation and mining
Urbanisation, migration and conflict
Climate change, trade and tourism
Economic development, rising population and technology
10-resource-management.explain: Economic development, population growth and technology. GNI per person and energy consumption per person are positively correlated across the world's countries.

10-resource-management.q: What share of the world's unexploited natural gas is thought to lie in the Arctic?
10-resource-management.explain: 30% — which is why the Arctic is becoming politically contested as the ice retreats, linking energy insecurity to conflict and to risk in a sensitive environment.

10-resource-management.q: Which of these is NOT one of the four factors affecting energy supply named by the specification?
options: Population density
Cost of exploitation and production
Physical factors
Technology
10-resource-management.explain: The four are physical factors, cost of exploitation and production, technology, and political factors. Population affects demand, not supply.

10-resource-management.q: What makes tidal power fundamentally different from wind and solar?
options: It produces no carbon dioxide
It is predictable, because tidal cycles are known years in advance
It can be built anywhere on a coast
It has no environmental impact
10-resource-management.explain: Predictability. Wind and solar are intermittent and so need backup capacity; tides are astronomical and can be planned into the grid. The 2023 report says understanding reliability separated the best answers.

10-resource-management.q: Which renewable source is described as effectively constant, 24 hours a day?
options: Wind
Solar
Wave
Geothermal
10-resource-management.explain: Geothermal, generated by heat stored deep in the Earth, with a tiny surface footprint — but only economic where hot rock is near the surface, so geographically very restricted.

10-resource-management.q: By how much has Brazil reduced its petrol consumption by introducing bio-ethanol?
10-resource-management.explain: 40%. Biomass uses recently absorbed carbon and can use waste, but monoculture for biofuel reduces biodiversity and competes with food crops for land.

10-resource-management.q: A disadvantage of hydro-electric power in upland areas is that…
options: large areas of land are flooded behind the dam
it produces greenhouse gases while generating
output cannot be controlled
it only works at night
10-resource-management.explain: Flooding valleys displaces people and drowns habitat. HEP's advantage is that it is reliable and output can be raised within minutes to match demand.

10-resource-management.q: The Camisea project in Peru extracts which fossil fuel?
options: Coal
Natural gas
Oil shale
Crude oil
10-resource-management.explain: Natural gas, from the Camisea region of the Peruvian Amazon, piped across the Andes to the coast. Gas is the cleanest fossil fuel, with 45% less CO₂.

10-resource-management.q: How much could Peru earn from Camisea exports over the project's life?
options: US$51,000 over 20 years
US$4 billion over 10 years
US$340 million over 30 years
US$34 billion over 30 years
10-resource-management.explain: US$34 billion over the 30-year life. US$4 billion is the separate saving in Peru's own energy costs; US$51,000 is the Chambamontera community's contribution.

10-resource-management.q: Which is a disadvantage of the Camisea project?
options: It employs only 120 people
Clearing routes for the pipelines has led to landslides
It raised Peru's energy costs
It uses more CO₂-intensive fuel than coal
10-resource-management.explain: Removing forest removes the roots binding steep Andean slopes. Other disadvantages: deforestation destroying habitat, impacts on indigenous tribes who may lack immunity to developers' diseases, and controversial fracking.

10-resource-management.q: The Chambamontera scheme in Peru is…
options: a natural gas pipeline
a large hydro-electric dam
a micro-hydro scheme in the Andes
a solar farm on the coast
10-resource-management.explain: A micro-hydro scheme in the Andes mountains, supported by the charity Practical Action, built because isolated communities are cut off from the main electricity network.

10-resource-management.q: How much did the Chambamontera community contribute to the cost of its scheme?
options: Nothing — it was fully funded by Practical Action
US$510,000 in total, about $7,500 per family
US$5,100 in total, about $75 per family
US$51,000 in total, about $750 per family
10-resource-management.explain: US$51,000, about $750 per family. Paying for it gives the community ownership and the incentive to maintain it — the logic of intermediate technology.

10-resource-management.q: Which outcome of the Chambamontera scheme is specifically recorded?
options: A new road to the nearest city
Electric street lighting, improving quality of life and economic opportunities
A hospital built by the Peruvian government
Free electricity for every household
10-resource-management.explain: Reliable electricity and electric street lighting, alongside renewable generation, low environmental impact, and low maintenance and running costs.

10-resource-management.q: A sustainable energy supply is defined by AQA as the combination of…
options: nuclear power and renewables
renewable sources only
energy savings, efficiency measures and technologies, and renewable energy sources
imported energy and domestic fossil fuels
10-resource-management.explain: Savings are listed first, which is why energy conservation counts as a way of achieving a sustainable supply even though it generates nothing — reducing demand moves the supply-demand balance exactly as new capacity would.

11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.q: How are the 76 marks on Paper 3 divided?
options: 38 marks for Section A and 38 for Section B
37 marks for Section A issue evaluation and 39 for Section B fieldwork
25 marks for Section A, 25 for Section B and 26 for skills
46 marks for Section A and 30 for Section B
11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.explain: Section A issue evaluation is 37 marks, Section B fieldwork is 39. The paper is 1 hour 15 minutes and 30% of the GCSE, with 6 of the 76 marks for spelling, punctuation and grammar.

11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.q: Where are the 6 SPaG marks on Paper 3 awarded?
options: Spread evenly across every question worth 4 marks or more
All six on the Section A decision question
On the two 6-mark discussion questions
Three on the Section A 9-marker and three on the Section B 9-marker
11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.explain: The front of the paper names exactly two questions for SPaG — the Section A 9-marker and the Section B familiar-fieldwork 9-marker — at 3 marks each. That is 6 of the 76, which is why paragraphing and geographical terminology matter on those two answers specifically.

11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.q: How long before the exam is the pre-release resources booklet issued, and what happens to your annotated copy?
options: Twelve weeks before; you take your annotated copy into the exam
Six weeks before; you memorise it because you get nothing in the exam
On the morning of the exam, with reading time
Twelve weeks before; you hand it back and get a clean copy in the exam
11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.explain: Twelve weeks (the 2026 booklet was issued on Thursday 19 March 2026). You work through and annotate it in class, but a clean, unmarked copy is issued in the exam room. That is why the twelve weeks are for annotating, categorising and ranking rather than memorising.

11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.q: A Section A answer that selects exactly the right sentence from the resources booklet and copies it across is marked at…
options: Level 3, because the evidence is appropriate
Level 2, because selecting evidence shows understanding
Level 1, because copying is not developing or evaluating
Zero, because quoting the booklet is not allowed
11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.explain: Every Paper 3 mark scheme says the same thing: copying is Level 1 even when the copied material is correct. Developing the point — 'this means that…' — reaches Level 2, and linking points from across the booklet to support a judgement reaches Level 3.

11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.q: Which assessment objective dominates Paper 3?
options: AO1, knowledge of locations, places and processes
AO2, understanding of geographical concepts
AO3, interpreting, analysing and evaluating information to make judgements
AO4 alone, the selection and use of skills
11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.explain: Paper 3 is nearly all AO3 with a substantial AO4 element — the 9-markers are marked AO3 6 / AO4 3. That is why the paper rewards judgement and skills rather than recall, and why the pre-release booklet can be in front of you without making the paper easy.

11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.q: In a Paper 3 Section A question that names no specific place, answering entirely through the booklet's case-study location is described by examiners as…
options: self-limiting, because the general question wants wider course understanding
the safest approach, because the resources are the only permitted evidence
worth full marks, as long as the detail is accurate
an automatic Level 1 cap
11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.explain: The 2023 report names this explicitly. Some questions tie to the location (the Cayman Islands questions) and some are broad topic discussions, where answers bringing in wider learning — economic leakage, seasonality, ecotourism — scored highest. Narrowing a general question to the location closes off marks without being wrong.

11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.q: In the 2026 pre-release booklet, which figure carries the specific proposed scheme and the stakeholders arguing about it?
options: Figure 1, water supply and demand in the UK
Figure 2, water futures
Figure 3, the proposed Lincolnshire reservoir
There is no such figure; the stakeholders are in the question paper
11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.explain: The three figures always do three jobs: Figure 1 the general problem with the national statistics, Figure 2 the possible solutions (plus the OS map of the site), Figure 3 the specific proposal with the stakeholder views. The 9-mark decision question is always set on Figure 3.

11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.q: What proportion of water supply in England comes from surface water?
11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.explain: Surface water is 64% of supply in England and 93% in Wales; the rest comes from groundwater, and England and Wales have 2259 groundwater sources against Scotland's 86. UK water companies supply over 16 billion litres a day in total.

11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.q: Of the projected increase in water demand in England between 2020 and 2050, how much falls in the South East?
11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.explain: The South East takes 50% of the increase, against the West 20%, Central and East 18%, and the North and South West 6% each. This is the key figure because the South East is also the driest region, receiving under 800 mm of rainfall a year — demand is growing fastest exactly where the resource is scarcest.

11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.q: Which single use accounts for the largest share of household water use in England?
options: Flushing toilets, at 30%
Personal washing, at 25%
Washing machines, at 21%
Garden use, at 7%
11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.explain: Toilets 30%, personal washing 25%, washing machines 21%, washing up 8%, garden 7%, drinking 4%, other 5%. Because flushing is the largest slice, rainwater harvesting into an underground tank used for flushing is the strongest single household measure.

11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.q: Roughly how much water is lost to leakage in England each day, and what share of supply is that?
options: Over 3 billion litres a day, about 20% of supply
140 to 150 million litres a day, about 2% of supply
16 billion litres a day, all of supply
4 billion litres a day, about 50% of supply
11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.explain: Over 3 billion litres a day, approximately 20% of supply. It is the residents' strongest argument against needing a new reservoir at all — the cheapest water available is water already treated and paid for. (140 to 150 million litres a day is the Thames desalination plant's output.)

11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.q: Serious water pollution incidents in England rose from 263 in 2020 to 325 in 2021. What is the percentage increase?
11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.explain: Percentage change divides by the ORIGINAL value: 62 ÷ 263 × 100 = 24%, the figure the booklet quotes. Dividing by the new value gives 19% and loses the mark — the commonest arithmetic error in this topic.

11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.q: How much water would the proposed Lincolnshire reservoir supply, and to how many homes?
options: 55 million litres a day to 175 000 homes
16 billion litres a day to the whole of eastern England
140 litres a day to 2000 homes
Up to 166 million litres a day to 500 000 homes
11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.explain: Up to 166 million litres a day to 500 000 homes, from a reservoir holding 55 million cubic metres. The 175 000 figure is the number of new homes planned in Lincolnshire over five years, and 140 litres a day is average personal consumption — don't mix them up.

11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.q: How would the proposed Lincolnshire reservoir be filled?
options: By desalinating water from the North Sea
By pumping groundwater from local aquifers all year round
By taking water from the Trent and Witham in winter when flows are highest
By rainwater harvesting across the catchment
11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.explain: Winter water is taken from the River Trent and River Witham when levels are highest, stored, then treated and supplied in the hotter summer months when river levels are low and demand is high. An overflow drain manages levels and reduces winter flood risk — which is why the scheme counts as climate-change adaptation.

11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.q: Which figure is the economic case for the Lincolnshire reservoir?
options: £2.6 billion of direct and indirect investment in the area
£55 million of government grant funding
2000 new permanent jobs on the reservoir
£166 million a year in water bills
11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.explain: £2.6 billion of direct and indirect investment, plus thousands of visitors a year using the sailing, wind surfing, cycling and walking facilities and spending with local businesses. The 2000 figure is the number of local people who signed the petition against the scheme.

11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.q: Why is the National Farmers Union's response the most useful single source in the 2026 booklet?
options: It is the only source with statistics in it
It opposes the scheme outright, so it supplies the whole negative case
It supports expanding water supply while warning about local harm, so it supplies both halves of a paragraph
It is written by the Environment Agency
11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.explain: The NFU fully supports expanding water infrastructure as a response to climate change and population growth, and says farms will benefit from the extra water — while warning that large-scale schemes significantly harm local farm businesses and communities and insisting local people be involved at every stage. A source on both sides gives you the evaluation for free.

11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.q: What is the title of John's physical geography fieldwork enquiry?
options: To what extent has the Olympic Regeneration of Stratford been successful?
Evaluate the success of groynes as a method of coastal management on Brighton beach
How does beach material change along the Brighton coastline?
Are sea walls more effective than groynes at Brighton?
11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.explain: The exact wording matters, because the examiners insist the answers must visibly reflect the aim in the title you write on the paper. The school's advice is to learn this enquiry for the 9-marker, because it is the more straightforward of the two to analyse.

11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.q: At what interval were the Brighton beach slope profiles measured, and what sampling method is that?
options: Every 1 m, random sampling
Every 5 m, stratified sampling
At three chosen spots, opportunity sampling
Every 2 m, systematic sampling
11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.explain: Every 2 m, measured from just above the breaking waves inland to the sea wall — systematic sampling, because the readings are taken at regular intervals. The justification is that 2 m gave enough detail of sediment build-up while staying quick enough to repeat on three adjacent groynes.

11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.q: Which four variables did the Brighton bi-polar analysis survey score?
options: Buildings, traffic, open space and general quality
Vulnerability to erosion, aesthetic value, lifespan, and disturbance to natural processes and habitats
Litter, vandalism, safety and green space
Width, height, gradient and sediment size
11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.explain: Those four, scored from -3 to +3, comparing the groynes with the sea wall. (Buildings, traffic, open space and general quality were the Stratford environmental quality survey's categories — a classic mix-up.)

11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.q: What did the Brighton slope profiles actually show?
options: More sediment on the downdrift (east) side and a deficit updrift
More sediment on the updrift (west) side and a clear deficit downdrift (east)
An equal amount of sediment either side of each groyne
No measurable difference, so the hypothesis was rejected
11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.explain: Longshore drift at Brighton runs west to east, so west is updrift. Sediment was trapped on the west side and depleted on the east, which is the evidence that the groynes are interrupting longshore drift and building a protective beach — the conclusion the title asked for.

11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.q: Which site scored highest in John's Stratford environmental quality survey, and with what score?
options: Site A, near Hackney Wick station, with +23
Site E, Westfield, with +17
Site C, East Village, with +31
Site B, the London Blossom Garden, with +23
11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.explain: Site B, the London Blossom Garden, at +23. Site A near Hackney Wick station scored lowest for building quality — it is peripheral to the park, grew from the 1990s with artists in converted warehouses, and has graffiti and more traffic. The contrast is the evidence that regeneration has been successful but uneven.

11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.q: What is the single biggest weakness of the Stratford questionnaire data?
options: The questions were all closed, so no qualitative data was collected
The sample was three people per site on one weekday, with no stratification by age
No one was willing to answer, so the sample was empty
It was collected in winter, so responses were unusually negative
11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.explain: Three people at each of five sites, one sunny weekday in the middle of the day — so residents were likely at work and tourists over-represented, and no age groups were deliberately sampled. Stratified sampling and a weekend visit would have fixed it. Q3 was an open question, so qualitative data was collected.

11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.q: How did John's class reduce the subjectivity of the Stratford environmental quality survey scores?
options: By taking a group average of the total score for each site, removing outliers
By using only one observer at every site
By discarding any site where scores disagreed
By converting the scores into percentages
11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.explain: A group average of totals removes the influence of outliers and improves accuracy and reliability. The other standard fix, from the fieldwork workbook, is a standardisation survey at one agreed point with everyone adjusting their scores to the group average before starting.

11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.q: 'Accurate', 'reliable' and 'valid' mean different things. Which set of definitions is right?
options: Accurate = repeatable; reliable = close to the true value; valid = officially approved
Accurate = quantitative; reliable = qualitative; valid = statistically significant
They are interchangeable terms for good data
Accurate = close to the true value; reliable = repeatable; valid = the conclusion is genuinely supported
11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.explain: Accuracy is about the measurement, reliability about repeatability, validity about the conclusion. The 2023 examiner's report found most candidates described their results or limitations but never linked them to the validity of the conclusion, and so stalled at Level 2 on the 9-marker. Write the chain: accuracy, therefore reliability, therefore validity.

11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.q: In a Section B question, 'suggest how the method could be ADAPTED' means…
options: suggest an additional data collection method, such as a questionnaire
change the method that is already shown in the figure
redesign the whole enquiry with a new hypothesis
explain why the method was chosen in the first place
11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.explain: The 2022 mark scheme explicitly refused credit for suggesting questionnaires on an 'adapt' question, because the answer had to reference the methods already in the figure. 'Additional' is the word that invites a new method — and in 2023 it also refused credit for repeating a question the figure had already asked.

11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.q: Which presentation technique is the right choice for investigating the relationship between two variables, such as river width and maximum depth?
options: A dispersion graph
An isoline map
A scattergraph
A pie chart
11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.explain: A scattergraph, with a line of best fit if you need to interpolate or extrapolate. A dispersion graph shows the spread of repeated readings at each site, an isoline map joins points of equal value, and a pie chart shows the composition of one whole. The 2023 report says only a very small proportion of candidates got the 'which technique' question right.

11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.q: On an OS map, what does the grid reference 1337 identify?
options: A point 100 m into the square, measured from the north-east corner
The square at easting 37, northing 13
The 1 km grid square whose south-west corner is easting 13, northing 37
A spot height of 1337 m
11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.explain: Eastings before northings — along the corridor, then up the stairs. Four figures name a whole 1 km square by its south-west corner; six figures divide that square into tenths and locate a point to 100 m. Each square is 1 km by 1 km, so it is also 1 km², which gives you distance and area for free.

11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.q: A question asks you to 'describe the physical geography' of an area on an OS map. What should the answer be about?
options: Roads, railways, settlements and named buildings
Relief and drainage — height, slope, rivers, lakes, ponds and woodland
The land uses shown in the key
The population density of the settlements
11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.explain: Relief and drainage. The 2022 examiner's report says very few candidates appeared to understand the term at all, and most wrote about human features. Level 1 is 'high land, low land and a river'; Level 2 needs precision — the slope, the height of the land, and the direction of flow of the rivers.

11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.q: Twelve areas score 4, 6, 6, 2, 9, 3, 10, 1, 5, 8, 10, 1 for housing quality. What is the best answer about the mode?
options: The mode is 1, because that is the lowest value
The mode is 10, because it appears most often
The data is trimodal — 1, 6 and 10 each appear twice — so the mode cannot usefully be calculated
The mode is 5.5, the same as the median
11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.explain: Exactly the point the 2019 mark scheme wanted: 'The mode cannot be calculated / trimodal / 1, 6, 10.' Saying so is creditworthy, not a failure. For the record, mean 5.41, median 5.5, range 9, interquartile range 6.

11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.q: Why might the interquartile range be more useful than the range, and when is no measure of central tendency much use at all?
options: The IQR describes the middle 50% so ignores extremes; and averages are little use when the enquiry is about differences between places
The IQR is easier to calculate; and averages are useless with fewer than ten readings
The IQR includes every value; and averages fail only when data is qualitative
The IQR is the same as the median; and averages are always the best measure
11-paper-3-issue-evaluation-and-fieldwor.explain: The range is set entirely by the two most extreme readings, while the IQR (upper quartile minus lower quartile) describes the spread of the middle 50% — which is why the 2019 mark scheme offers it as a better alternative. The deeper point from that mark scheme: measures of central tendency 'have limited use… since it is really about identifying differences and patterns' — collapsing twelve areas into one number destroys what the enquiry set out to find.
